PROJECT NO. 58481

RULEMAKING TO IMPLEMENT LARGE § PUBLIC UTILITY COMMISSION
LOAD INTERCONNECTION STANDARDS §§
UNDER PURA §37.0561 § OF TEXAS

Provident Inc. Comments on Staff Discussion Draft
New 16 TAC §25.194

I. INTRODUCTION

Provident Inc. appreciates the opportunity to submit comments on the Staff
Discussion Draft of new 16 TAC §25.194 (Large Load Interconnection Standards). Provident
thanks Commission Staff for the significant effort invested in developing a comprehensive
and structured framework to implement Senate Bill 6 and new PURA §37.0561.

Provident recognizes and supports the Commission’s objective of establishing
clearer, more disciplined interconnection standards for large loads in ERCOT. The
unprecedented scale and pace of large-load growth—particularly from data centers and
advanced computing—requires a regulatory framework that is transparent, predictable, and
durable. Staff's discussion draft represents a meaningful step toward that goal.

Provident is an active Texas-based developer of large-scale, powered-land data
center campuses with deep roots in the state and a track record of responsible,
infrastructure-driven development. In its work supporting large-load and data center
projects, Provident frequently serves as a trusted advisor to multiple Tier 1 hyperscale
customers on power, siting, and delivery matters. Provident offers these comments from the
perspective of a responsible developer committed to prudent, safe, and reliable development

outcomes and long-term good-faith engagement with utilities, ERCOT, and the State of Texas.

Provident Comments - Page 1

 Il. GENERAL COMMENTS

Provident supports the need for this rulemaking and agrees that SB 6 appropriately
balances three essential objectives: (1) maintaining system reliability, (2) minimizing
stranded infrastructure risk, and (3) supporting continued business development in Texas.

Provident commends Commission Staff for advancing a framework that introduces
greater discipline into the large-load interconnection process while improving transparency
and predictability for all stakeholders. In particular, Provident supports the use of financial
security as a tool to demonstrate project seriousness and discourage speculative or inflated
interconnection requests.

Large-load interconnection is inherently a coordinated, multi-party process involving
developers, end-use customers, transmission and distribution utilities, ERCOT, and
regulators. No single participant controls all elements of timing, cost, feasibility, or system
impact. Successful outcomes depend on alignment across this broader ecosystem, including
realistic load forecasting, timely infrastructure development, and transparent planning
assumptions.

As demand from data centers, artificial intelligence, and other advanced computing
applications accelerates, Texas’s regulatory framework will play a meaningful role in
determining where this critical infrastructure is ultimately deployed. These facilities support
industries that are increasingly strategic in nature, with global competition for investment
and deployment occurring at both the state and national level. While strong safeguards are
necessary to protect grid reliability, requirements that are overly rigid, front-loaded, or
misaligned with development realities risk distorting planning signals and discouraging
responsible investment.

Accordingly, the Commission’s approach should promote shared accountability

across all participants in the large-load interconnection process while avoiding structures

Provident Comments -~ Page 2

 that concentrate risk or incentives in a manner that leads to speculative behavior, non-
representative load requests, or inefficient use of planning resources.

At the same time, it is critical that the rule be calibrated correctly. Overly punitive or
inflexible requirements risk creating unintended consequences, including discouraging
responsible development, incentivizing non-representative load requests, and diverting

capital away from infrastructure execution in Texas.

III. Financial Security Is Necessary but Must Be Properly Calibrated

Provident supports the Commission’s proposal to require financial security for large-
load interconnection requests as a means of discouraging speculative activity and promoting
accountability. Financial security can be an effective tool when structured to reflect actual

system risk and development realities.

IV. Recommended Changes to Draft 16 TAC §25.194
§25.194(a) - Purpose and Scope

Provident recommends clarifying that the purpose of the rule is not only to deter
speculative requests, but also to promote accurate and representative load forecasts that
reflect realistic development timelines. Emphasizing planning accuracy will help ensure that

the rule supports both system reliability and efficient infrastructure investment.

§25.194(c)(1), (e)(1), and (h)(1) - Transparency and End-Use Customer Disclosure
Provident supports limited, standardized disclosure regarding whether a large-load
request is supported by an identified end user once interconnection feasibility and power

availability have been reasonably established. At that stage, identification of an end-use

Provident Comments - Page 3

 customer can provide additional certainty regarding anticipated load magnitude, ramp
schedule, and operating characteristics that may assist ERCOT and utility planning.

Requiring a direct end user disclosure or contractual commitment prior to
confirmation of power availability would be unreasonable and would effectively create a two-
tier interconnection framework that favors only end-use applications over developer-led
projects. Such an approach does not reflect how large-load projects are actually developed
and would impose disproportionate risk on real Texas-based developers who must secure
land, infrastructure, and interconnection feasibility before the end-use commitments can be
finalized.

Some degree of uncertainty is inherent in large-load development and is not unique
to developer-led projects. Even end-use companies often lack full certainty—years in
advance—regarding the ultimate configuration, timing, corporate ownership, or load profile
of large, multi-phase campuses. Accordingly, the absence of a fully executed end user
customer agreement or finalized load definition before both interconnection and power
availability have been confirmed should not be treated as a deficiency or used to differentiate
among applicants.

Where a developer is advancing a project on behalf of, or in coordination with, an end-
user—and is responsible for site control, tenant build-out, and infrastructure design—such
requests should be evaluated on a consistent basis with end-use customer-led applications.
Disclosure requirements should be calibrated to support system planning without requiring
premature commitments or commercially sensitive information and should focus on
identifying good-faith projects with a credible execution path rather than privileging only an

end user over the development entities that serve them.

Provident Comments - Page 4

 Accordingly, Provident recommends that the disclosure requirement regarding site
control in subsection (h)(1) should mirror the site control disclosure requirements in
subsections (c){1) and (e)(1).

§25,194(e)(4 - 6) - Project Readiness and Queue Integrity

Provident supports the inclusion of project readiness considerations to protect queue
integrity and ensure that limited planning resources are directed toward viable projects.
Objective indicators such as site control, demonstrated development capability, financial
capacity, and alignment with realistic infrastructure timelines can help achieve this goal
without running into the unintended consequences described above that required customer
disclosure may cause.

Any readiness framework should be applied in a technology-neutral and non-
discriminatory manner and should not favor any particular business model or market

participant.

§25.194(e)(8) - Financial Security Requirements

Provident supports the concept of requiring financial security to ensure that costs
incurred to interconnect a large-load customer are borne by the customer and not Texans at
large. However, requiring financial security calculated on the basis of the full proposed peak
demand to be posted in a single upfront payment before any large load interconnection study
is submitted to ERCOT is inconsistent with how large-load projects are developed and
studied.

At the pre-study stage, there is inherent uncertainty regarding system conditions,
network constraints, and the scope of facilities that may ultimately be required. Before any

study work is completed, it is not yet known which transmission elements must be evaluated,

Provident Comments - Page 5

 upgraded, or right-sized. In this context, an upfront financial security requirement of $50,000
per MW is not reflective of demonstrated cost exposure at this phase of the process.

Provident recommends a financial security range of $10,000-$15,000 per MW at the
pre-study phase as a more reasonable and proportionate approach, with additional security
layered in as system impacts, cost exposure, and required facilities become better defined
through the study process.

Large-load projects, including hyperscale developments, are inherently phased, and
it is neither realistic nor efficient to develop the full requested load simultaneously.
Accordingly, Provident recommends a tiered financial security framework that reflects both
the total peak demand of the proposed project and the timeline over which that demand is
proposed to ramp. For example, a proposed 500 MW project that plans to ramp over five
years should be required to post less upfront security than a project proposing to ramp the
same 500 MW over two years. Higher security for a faster ramp is appropriate, as such
projects present greater near-term stress to grid development and system planning.

This approach would encourage more accurate and credible ramp schedules, reduce
the creation of phantom load in near-term planning models, and better align financial
commitments with actual development risk.

Provident further recommends that the rule clearly define how posted financial
security will be held, applied, and released. Where a project receives study results or in-
service dates that materially undermine its viability, developers should have a clearly defined
off-ramp allowing withdrawal subject to a true-up of reasonable and documented costs, with

any remaining funds returned to the customer.

Provident Comments - Page 6

 IV. CONCLUSION

Provident appreciates the Commission’s leadership in addressing large-load
interconnection challenges and supports the timely adoption of proposed 16 TAC §25.194.
Properly structured, these standards can improve transparency, promote disciplined project
development, and reinforce the safety and reliability of the ERCOT system while providing
utilities and regulators the information needed for effective long-term planning.

By calibrating financial security requirements to reflect development realities,
clarifying end-use customer disclosure expectations, and recognizing the inherently
coordinated, multi-party nature of large-load development, the Commission can discourage
speculative activity without unintentionally constraining responsible investment. Provident
believes this balanced approach will help ensure Texas remains competitive in attracting
advanced computing, data center, and artificial intelligence infrastructure—industries that
are increasingly strategic to the state and national economy—while preserving the resilience
and integrity of the electric grid.

Respectfully submitted,

Jain es, Jr.

Dallas, Texas 75231

jhawes@provident.net

EXECUTIVE SUMMARY

through 16 TAC §25.194 and appreciates Staffs efforts to establish clearer large-load

Key Points

SB 6 Objectives
o SB 6 balances system reliability, mitigation of stranded infrastructure risk,
and economic development in Texas.
o Predictable interconnection standards are essential given accelerating large-
load growth.
Transparency and Disclosure
o End-use disclosure should occur only after interconnection feasibility and
power availability are established.
o Early disclosure would concentrate access among a small number of global
end users and exclude Texas-based developers.
o Developer- and end-user-led projects should be evaluated consistently.
Financial Security
o Financial security is appropriate to protect Texans from interconnection
costs.
o A $50,000 per MW upfront requirement is misaligned with phased
development.
o A $10,000-$15,000 per MW pre-study range is more appropriate, with
additional security layered as impacts are defined.
Phased Framework and Queue Integrity
o Large-load projects develop in phases and should not post full peak security
at the outset.
o Readiness requirements should be objective, technology-neutral, and
preserve queue integrity.

o The rule should define clear off-ramps and security release mechanisms.

I. INTRODUCTION

       Provident Inc. appreciates the opportunity to submit comments on the Staff

Discussion Draft of new 16 TAC §25.194 (Large Load Interconnection Standards). Provident

thanks Commission Staff for the significant effort invested in developing a comprehensive

and structured framework to implement Senate Bill 6 and new PURA §37.0561.

       Provident recognizes and supports the Commission's objective of establishing

clearer, more disciplined interconnection standards for large loads in ERCOT. The

unprecedented scale and pace of large-load growth-particularly from data centers and

advanced computing-requires a regulatory framework that is transparent, predictable, and

durable. Staff's discussion draft represents a meaningful step toward that goal.

       Provident is an active Texas-based developer of large-scale, powered-land data

center campuses with deep roots in the state and a track record of responsible,

infrastructure-driven development. In its work supporting large-load and data center

projects, Provident frequently serves as a trusted advisor to multiple Tier 1 hyperscale

customers on power, siting, and delivery matters. Provident offers these comments from the

perspective of a responsible developer committed to prudent, safe, and reliable development

outcomes and long-term good-faith engagement with utilities, ERCOT, and the State of Texas.




                                                               Provident Comments - Page 1
 II. GENERAL COMMENTS

       Provident supports the need for this rulemaking and agrees that SB 6 appropriately

balances three essential objectives: (1) maintaining system reliability, (2) minimizing

stranded infrastructure risk, and (3) supporting continued business development in Texas.

       Provident commends Commission Staff for advancing a framework that introduces

greater discipline into the large-load interconnection process while improving transparency

and predictability for all stakeholders. In particular, Provident supports the use of financial

security as a tool to demonstrate project seriousness and discourage speculative or inflated

interconnection requests.

       Large-load interconnection is inherently a coordinated, multi-party process involving

developers, end-use customers, transmission and distribution utilities, ERCOT,             and

regulators. No single participant controls all elements of timing, cost, feasibility, or system

impact. Successful outcomes depend on alignment across this broader ecosystem, including

realistic load forecasting, timely infrastructure development, and transparent planning

assumptions.

       As demand from data centers, artificial intelligence, and other advanced computing

applications accelerates, Texas's regulatory framework will play a meaningful role in

determining where this critical infrastructure is ultimately deployed. These facilities support

industries that are increasingly strategic in nature, with global competition for investment

and deployment occurring at both the state and national level. While strong safeguards are

necessary to protect grid reliability, requirements that are overly rigid, front-loaded, or

misaligned with development realities risk distorting planning signals and discouraging

responsible investment.

       Accordingly, the Commission's approach should promote shared accountability

across all participants in the large-load interconnection process while avoiding structures


                                                                Provident Comments - Page 2
 that concentrate risk or incentives in a manner that leads to speculative behavior, non-

representative load requests, or inefficient use of planning resources.

       At the same time, it is critical that the rule be calibrated correctly. Overly punitive or

inflexible requirements risk creating unintended consequences, including discouraging

responsible development, incentivizing non-representative load requests, and diverting

capital away from infrastructure execution in Texas.




III. Financial Security Is Necessary but Must Be Properly Calibrated

       Provident supports the Commission's proposal to require financial security for large-

load interconnection requests as a means of discouraging speculative activity and promoting

accountability Financial security can be an effective tool when structured to reflect actual

system risk and development realities.



IV. Recommended Changes to Draft 16 TAC §25.194

§25.194(a) - Purpose and Scope

       Provident recommends clarifying that the purpose of the rule is not only to deter

speculative requests, but also to promote accurate and representative load forecasts that

reflect realistic development timelines. Emphasizing planning accuracy will help ensure that

the rule supports both system reliability and efficient infrastructure investment.



§25.194(c)(11 (e)(1), and (h)(1) - Transparency and End-Use Customer Disclosure

       Provident supports limited, standardized disclosure regarding whether a large-load

request is supported by an identified end user once interconnection feasibility and power

availability have been reasonably established. At that stage, identification of an end-use




                                                                 Provident Comments - Page 3
 customer can provide additional certainty regarding anticipated load magnitude, ramp

schedule, and operating characteristics that may assist ERCOT and utility planning.

        Requiring a direct end user disclosure or contractual commitment prior to

confirmation of power availability would be unreasonable and would effectively create a two-

tier interconnection framework that favors only end-use applications over developer-led

projects. Such an approach does not reflect how large-load projects are actually developed

and would impose disproportionate risk on real Texas-based developers who must secure

land, infrastructure, and interconnection feasibility before the end-use commitments can be

finalized.

        Some degree of uncertainty is inherent in large-load development and is not unique

to developer-led projects. Even end-use companies often lack full certainty-years in

advance-regarding the ultimate configuration, timing, corporate ownership, or load profile

of large, multi-phase campuses. Accordingly, the absence of a fully executed end user

customer agreement or finalized load definition before both interconnection and power

availability have been confirmed should not be treated as a deficiency or used to differentiate

among applicants.

        Where a developer is advancing a project on behalf of, or in coordination with, an end-

user-and is responsible for site control, tenant build-out, and infrastructure design-such

requests should be evaluated on a consistent basis with end-use customer-led applications.

Disclosure requirements should be calibrated to support system planning without requiring

premature commitments or commercially sensitive information and should focus on

identifying good-faith projects with a credible execution path rather than privileging only an

end user over the development entities that serve them.




                                                                Provident Comments - Page 4
         Accordingly, Provident recommends that the disclosure requirement regarding site

control in subsection (h) (1) should mirror the site control disclosure requirements in

subsections (c)(1) and (e)(1).

§25„194(e)(4 - 6) - Project Readiness and Queue Integrity

        Provident supports the inclusion of project readiness considerations to protect queue

integrity and ensure that limited planning resources are directed toward viable projects.

Objective indicators such as site control, demonstrated development capability, financial

capacity, and alignment with realistic infrastructure timelines can help achieve this goal

without running into the unintended consequences described above that required customer

disclosure may cause.

        Any readiness framework should be applied in a technology-neutral and non-

discriminatory manner and should not favor any particular business model or market

participant.



§25.194(e)(8) - Financial Security Requirements

        Provident supports the concept of requiring financial security to ensure that costs

incurred to interconnect a large-load customer are borne by the customer and not Texans at

large. However, requiring financial security calculated on the basis of the full proposed peak

demand to be posted in a single upfront payment before any large load interconnection study

is submitted to ERCOT is inconsistent with how large-load projects are developed and

studied.

        At the pre-study stage, there is inherent uncertainty regarding system conditions,

network constraints, and the scope of facilities that may ultimately be required. Before any

study work is completed, it is not yet known which transmission elements must be evaluated,




                                                               Provident Comments - Page 5
 upgraded, or right-sized. In this context, an upfront financial security requirement of $50,000

per MW is not reflective of demonstrated cost exposure at this phase o f the process.

       Provident recommends a financial security range of $10,000-$15,000 per MW at the

pre-study phase as a more reasonable and proportionate approach, with additional security

layered in as system impacts, cost exposure, and required facilities become better defined

through the study process.

       Large-load projects, including hyperscale developments, are inherently phased, and

it is neither realistic nor efficient to develop the full requested load simultaneously.

Accordingly, Provident recommends a tiered financial security framework that reflects both

the total peak demand of the proposed project and the timeline over which that demand is

proposed to ramp. For example, a proposed 500 MW project that plans to ramp over five

years should be required to post less upfront security than a project proposing to ramp the

same 500 MW over two years. Higher security for a faster ramp is appropriate, as such

projects present greater near-term stress to grid development and system planning.

       This approach would encourage more accurate and credible ramp schedules, reduce

the creation of phantom load in near-term planning models, and better align financial

commitments with actual development risk.

       Provident further recommends that the rule clearly define how posted financial

security will be held, applied, and released. Where a project receives study results or in-

service dates that materially undermine its viability, developers should have a clearly defined

off-ramp allowing withdrawal subject to a true-up of reasonable and documented costs, with

any remaining funds returned to the customer.

 IV. CONCLUSION

        Provident appreciates the Commission's leadership in addressing large-load

interconnection challenges and supports the timely adoption of proposed 16 TAC §25.194.

Properly structured, these standards can improve transparency, promote disciplined project

development, and reinforce the safety and reliability of the ERCOT system while providing

utilities and regulators the information needed for effective long-term planning.

        By calibrating financial security requirements to reflect development realities,

clarifying end-use customer disclosure expectations, and recognizing the inherently

coordinated, multi-party nature of large-load development, the Commission can discourage

speculative activity without unintentionally constraining responsible investment. Provident

believes this balanced approach will help ensure Texas remains competitive in attracting

advanced computing, data center, and artificial intelligence infrastructure-industries that

are increasingly strategic to the state and national economy-while preserving the resilience

and integrity of the electric grid.
